title: Your Voice Agent is Just a Walkie Talkie — Neil Zeghidour, Gradium
talk_summary: A voice-AI research talk tracing voice agents from Siri's cascaded STT→NLU→TTS pipeline through speech-to-speech models to full-duplex multi-stream models, arguing that adding modalities to a model steals capacity from intelligence. The speaker advocates a hybrid architecture: a small, cheap, natural full-duplex interface that delegates reasoning/tool-calling to a background text LLM.

takeaways.technique: Split cheap interface model from expensive reasoning model
takeaways.what_they_do: Use a small, cheap model for the high-frequency, low-intelligence interaction layer and asynchronously delegate all reasoning/tool-calling to a background frontier text model, so you don't pay frontier prices for trivial turns.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's a loss of money to do chit-chat with gigantic speech-to-speech models that can resolve differential equations

takeaways.technique: Keep backend model swappable (avoid modality/provider lock-in)
takeaways.what_they_do: They argue against end-to-end single-model systems partly because you lose the ability to switch the intelligence backend; cite OpenAI's voice mode being stuck on GPT-4o long after newer text models shipped.
takeaways.evidence_quote: until recently the AdSense voice mode from OpenAI was powered by GPT-4o, despite the fact that there have been several generations of the text model since then

takeaways.technique: Capacity budget is zero-sum across capabilities
takeaways.what_they_do: Explains that a fixed-weight model asked to handle more modalities spends capacity on them, reducing intelligence — a general argument that adding scope to a fixed budget degrades the core task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there is a cost of adding a new modality to a text model that is going to be paid in in intelligence
